Under ADR-045 (still a draft), a re:cinq npm package is published by a GitHub Actions release workflow. The workflow runs on a push of a `v*` tag, and it can also be started with `workflow_dispatch`. It has `permissions: contents: read` and `id-token: write`. It installs `npm@^11.5.1` first, because OIDC trusted publishing needs that version or newer and Node 22 ships an older npm. Then it runs `npm publish --provenance --access public`. `--provenance` is left out only for private-source repos such as bowman-ui.

Auth is npm Trusted Publishing over OIDC. A trusted publisher is registered on npmjs.com for the package, pointing at the repo and the release workflow. No `NPM_TOKEN` secret is used. The one exception is the very first publish of a new package name. It is done once with a short-lived token, and the token is revoked after the trusted publisher is registered. That is because registering a trusted publisher requires the package to already exist.

The package must also have the standard manifest: `@re-cinq` scope, Apache-2.0 license, ESM-only (`"type": "module"`), `files: ["dist"]`, an `exports` map, `publishConfig.access: public`, and a `repository` object. New workflows must also carry the PA-17 hardening: `persist-credentials: false` on checkout, `--ignore-scripts` on `npm ci`, job-scoped token permissions, and third-party actions pinned by commit SHA.

The release job compares the git tag with the committed `package.json` version first, and fails before publishing if they disagree. This comes from a past incident. Tags `v0.5.0` to `v0.7.0` published nothing, and npm stayed on `0.3.0` for nine weeks. npm's rejection of a duplicate version looks like an auth failure, so nobody investigated (ai-agent-subsystem#139). The guard turns that silent failure into a red job that names the fix. The reference implementation is `scripts/check-contracts-version.sh` in ai-agent-subsystem.

A later amendment (2026-10-24) adds a changelog rule. The `## [Unreleased]` heading becomes `## [X.Y.Z] - date` in the same commit as the `package.json` version bump that the guard compares against the tag.

judgements.reason: The answer covers the v*-tag GitHub Actions workflow running npm publish --provenance via OIDC Trusted Publishing with no NPM_TOKEN (except a short-lived token for the first publish), and explains that the tag/package.json guard exists because v0.5.0–v0.7.0 published nothing for nine weeks while npm's duplicate-version rejection looked like an auth failure.
